script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: OK, Niall, we need to get the method section of our proposal finished today. Shall we go through the procedure step by step, so we can draw the flow chart?

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: Good idea. So, step one is recruiting participants. We said forty students from the halls of residence.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: Right. In the pilot, we sent emails to everyone, and hardly anyone replied. Students just ignore university emails. Posters on the noticeboards weren't much better.

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: But when we got the student union to advertise it on their social media pages, we had thirty volunteers in a day. So for the main study, we'll recruit through the student union.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: Agreed. Then, step two, each participant records how much food they throw away. We talked about using a food diary, where they'd just estimate amounts.

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: But estimates are useless. People always say they waste less than they really do. So we'll give each participant a digital scale and they'll weigh everything before it goes in the bin.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: Yes. And then they enter the weights. Paper forms got lost in the pilot, didn't they?

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: Several did. So this time everyone types their figures straight into a shared spreadsheet online. We can check it every day and spot gaps.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: Good. Then the recording period. Originally we said two weeks.

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: But two weeks isn't long enough to capture a full shopping cycle. A lot of students only do a big shop every ten days or so. I think we should run it for three weeks, then hold the focus groups.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: Three weeks it is. And in the focus groups we discuss why food is wasted. From the pilot, the biggest cause seemed to be buying in bulk. Students buy the big multipacks because they're cheaper, and then half of it goes off before they can eat it.

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: That came up again and again. More than portion size or cooking skills, really.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: And the final step is comparing our figures with something. I'd suggested the national household survey, but that's about families, not students.

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: Right, so it'd be much more useful to compare with the records from the university's catering department. They weigh the waste from the dining halls every week, so we'd be comparing students cooking for themselves with students eating in the canteen.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: Brilliant. OK, the next section is about what went wrong in the pilot. We should be honest about the problems.

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: Well, the scales worked perfectly, so that's not an issue. And the number of participants, ten, was fine for a pilot.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: The main problem was that people forgot to record their waste, especially at weekends. Some days were just blank.

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: And the other big one was shared meals. When four flatmates cook a curry together and throw some away, whose waste is it? We couldn't divide it fairly between them.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: True. The questionnaire at the end was a bit long, but people still completed it, so I wouldn't call that a problem.

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: Fine. And finally, the recommendations section. We need to suggest two things the university could actually do.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: I was going to say cooking classes, but the university already runs those, and hardly anyone goes.

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: What about a food-sharing app? Students could post food they won't finish, and someone else in the building can collect it. There are free platforms we could adapt.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: Yes, I like that. And the other thing people mentioned in the pilot was that in shared fridges nobody knew whose food was whose, so things just sat there until they went off. If each student had their own labelled shelf, that would help a lot.

script.speaker: Niall
script.text: Definitely. Someone also suggested smaller fridges, but I think that would just annoy people. And discounts at the campus shop aren't really something we can recommend; that's a commercial decision.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: Agreed. So, the app and the labelled shelves. Let's write it up.
